name: lock-free-queue
intent: Pass work between concurrent threads through a shared FIFO whose enqueue and dequeue complete with atomic compare-and-swap instead of a mutex, so that a suspended thread cannot block the others and the queue itself stops being the contention bottleneck.
problem: A queue is the natural hand-off between producers and consumers, but a mutex-protected queue serialises every merge and drain on one lock: under load the lock becomes the throughput ceiling and its cache line ping-pongs between cores, while a thread preempted or page-faulted while holding it stalls every other producer and consumer - priority inversion and convoying that latency-sensitive or real-time work cannot tolerate. The trigger is a contended hand-off path where compare-and-swap (or LL/SC) is available and the lock's blocking behaviour - not the queue's capacity - is the problem.
context: Shared-memory concurrency on multi-core or multi-agent runtimes where several producers and consumers exchange work items through one FIFO and the queue operations are a material fraction of the hot path: thread pools and task runtimes, real-time audio or trading pipelines, telemetry buffers, network receive rings and callback hand-offs. Applies when an atomic read-modify-write primitive exists and removed storage can be reclaimed (garbage collection, hazard pointers, epochs/RCU, a type-stable pool, or a bounded array), and it forces an explicit decision about full and empty behaviour - the structure reports state instead of blocking.
benefits: A thread that is preempted, paged out or killed cannot block anyone else: at least one thread always completes an operation, so there is no held-lock failure mode and no priority inversion.

Hand-off scales with cores instead of serialising: producers and consumers mostly touch disjoint atomic words (head and tail live on separate cache lines), so throughput keeps rising in the region where one mutex saturates.

The hot path performs only atomic instructions and plain writes, which makes the pattern usable where taking a lock is forbidden or too slow - async-signal-safe hand-off, real-time threads and kernel-bypass receive paths.

Bounded ring realizations make the critical path allocation-free and cache-friendly: a fixed array of slots with per-slot sequence numbers removes node allocation and the allocator lock that comes with it.
Runtime robustness: a stalled thread leaves the structure usable, which is exactly why schedulers, work-stealing runtimes and message-passing runtimes build their internal queues this way.
tradeoffs: Correctness is subtle in a way a mutex never is: ABA, memory ordering and safe reclamation must all be solved, and leftover bugs surface as rare timing-dependent corruption rather than reproducible failures.

Unbounded variants cannot apply backpressure - the producer never waits - so overload turns into unbounded memory growth unless a bounded ring and an explicit full policy (fail, drop, overwrite, block) are added.
Lock-free is neither wait-free nor fair: individual threads can starve, and under heavy contention CAS retries waste work and can lose to a well-tuned mutex, especially when the lock is uncontended.

Operations do not compose: there is no way to hold the queue across a check-then-act sequence, so invariants spanning two operations or two objects need a different design (a lock, an actor, or a transaction).
Reclamation machinery costs something: deferred frees consume memory, grace periods consume latency, and calling a general-purpose allocator from the hot path hands the blocking straight back.

participants.responsibility: Publishes items with the enqueue operation; in a bounded ring it observes the full condition and applies the agreed policy instead of blocking.
Removes items with the dequeue operation and takes ownership of them; in a bounded ring it also publishes the freed slot for reuse.
The shared atomic words - head and tail pointers with tags, or push/pop tickets plus per-slot sequence numbers - whose updates are the only contended operations.
The linked nodes or fixed array of slots that hold the items; ownership transfers on dequeue, and the choice of storage decides whether the design allocates at all.

Decides when a removed node may be freed or reused (garbage collector, hazard pointers, epochs/RCU, type-stable pool, or per-slot sequence numbers); without one a node-based lock-free queue is unsound.
The bounded variant's rule for a full (and empty) queue - fail fast, drop, overwrite, or sleep/notify - because the structure itself never blocks the caller.

use_cases: Work distribution inside thread pools, task runtimes and work-stealing schedulers, where a stalled worker must not stall the scheduler (Go run queues, ForkJoinPool, rayon, thread-pool-executor).
Passing requests between an I/O, network or audio thread and a pool of processing threads, where blocking the producing thread is unacceptable (receive rings, market-data feeds, audio callbacks).
Telemetry and logging: many threads enqueue records into one buffer drained by a single flusher, usually as a bounded ring so the producing path stays allocation-free.
Message hand-off between threads or actors in languages without a channel runtime (C, C++, Java), where the queue object is the hand-off contract.
Real-time and embedded control loops that must not take a lock in the sampling path, typically as a wait-free single-producer/single-consumer ring.
LMAX Disruptor pattern: single-producer/multi-consumer ring buffer as the core of a financial exchange's event processing pipeline, achieving millions of events per second with deterministic latency.
Go channel internals: the select/poll mechanism and the underlying ring buffer in the Go runtime's implementation of concurrent channels.
Rust mpsc channel: the std::sync::mpsc implementation uses a lock-free ring for the synchronous slot and a growing linked list for the asynchronous case.
Network NIC receive rings: ring buffers between NIC hardware and the driver stack, where DMA descriptors are posted and consumed without OS-level locking.
Audio DSP graphs: lock-free rings connect processing nodes in real-time audio frameworks (e.g., REAPER SDK, VST3) to avoid blocking the audio thread.
Java's ConcurrentLinkedQueue: an unbounded, linked-node, non-blocking FIFO for many producers and consumers, suitable when garbage-collected reclamation and unbounded growth are acceptable.
.NET's ConcurrentQueue<T>: a thread-safe, lock-free FIFO whose Enqueue/TryDequeue operations let an application use the platform queue without custom node reclamation.
Rust crossbeam_queue: ArrayQueue provides a bounded lock-free MPMC ring while SegQueue provides an unbounded lock-free MPMC queue, making capacity and backpressure an explicit design choice.
avoid_when: Contention is low or the queue is not the bottleneck: a mutex-protected queue (a Monitor Object) is simpler and typically faster when uncontended.
Consumers must block when the queue is empty - the ordinary producer-consumer shape: a blocking queue with condition variables, or channels, expresses waiting directly.
The language exposes no compare-and-swap and no reclamation path (pure Python, Ruby without native extensions): use the stdlib lock-based queue or channels instead of emulating one.
One producer feeds one consumer: an SPSC ring with two indices and release/acquire stores (or a stdlib ringbuffer) is simpler than general MPMC machinery.
Throughput is dominated by payload size or downstream work: copying and cache effects dwarf the lock, so removing it buys nothing.
anti_patterns: Rewriting a working mutex-protected queue lock-free on the intuition that locks are slow, without a profile showing the lock is the bottleneck.
Hand-rolled Michael-Scott queues without safe memory reclamation (or without the double-width CAS the algorithm needs): latent use-after-free and ABA instead of a lock.
Using an unbounded lock-free queue as a mailbox between subsystems, turning overload into unbounded memory growth instead of backpressure.
Treating lock-free as wait-free and building latency guarantees on the assumption that every thread finishes in bounded steps.
Allocating and freeing nodes through a general-purpose allocator in the hot path, which hands the blocking straight back to the allocator.
design_principles: Measure before removing the lock: the simplest correct synchronisation that meets the budget wins (KISS/YAGNI applied to concurrency).
State the progress guarantee explicitly (wait-free, lock-free, obstruction-free) and which threads may starve.
Make the memory model explicit: each shared word has a documented ordering - release to publish, acquire to observe - instead of a blanket sequentially-consistent default.
Prefer bounded and allocation-free designs where the workload allows: bounding removes both the reclamation problem and the unbounded-growth failure mode.
Do not hand-roll what the platform already ships: standard queues encode years of memory-order and reclamation fixes.
best_practices: Use the platform queue first (ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ConcurrentQueue, boost::lockfree, crossbeam-queue, std::spsc_queue) and hand-roll only when a profile shows the lock is the bottleneck.
When hand-rolling, start from a published algorithm (Michael-Scott for MPMC, Vyukov's bounded ring for fixed capacity) and keep the pseudocode next to the code as a correctness reference.
Pair every node-based queue with a reclamation scheme — hazard pointers (safe for general use), epochs/RCU (low overhead, read-heavy), or a type-stable pool — before it reaches production.
Pad head, tail, and hot slot metadata onto separate cache lines (typically 64-byte alignment) to eliminate false sharing between producers and consumers.
Define the full/empty policy and shutdown semantics explicitly: fail, drop, overwrite, block with a CV, poison pill, closed flag, or drain-then-stop — and document which is the default.
Prefer bounded rings where the workload allows: bounding removes both the reclamation problem and the unbounded-growth failure mode; single-producer/single-consumer rings are wait-free and simpler.
Use memory_order_relaxed only where you can prove ordering is unnecessary; default to memory_order_seq_cst or explicit acquire/release until the hot path is proven by profiling.

Verify with the right tools: ThreadSanitizer (TSan) for data races, stress tests with many producers/consumers and injected faults, and model checkers (CDSChecker, GenMC, Relacy) for the memory-order-sensitive core.
Protect against compiler optimization: use compiler fences or the equivalent volatile atomic operations where the CPU memory model alone does not order the accesses.
Handle spurious CAS failures gracefully: exponential back-off or pause instructions (x86 pause, ARM yield) reduce contention waste without introducing blocking.
sources: Maged M. Michael & Michael L. Scott, "Simple, Fast, and Practical Non-Blocking and Blocking Concurrent Queue Algorithms", PODC 1996 (revised in JPDC 1998) — the CAS/LL-SC non-blocking queue algorithm that most modern lock-free queues implement; pseudocode at https://www.cs.rochester.edu/research/synchronization/pseudocode/queues.html.

Maurice Herlihy & Nir Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming — the wait-free / lock-free / obstruction-free progress hierarchy and systematic treatment of linearizability, consensus numbers, and the implementation of universal synchronization primitives.

Dmitry Vyukov, "Bounded MPMC Queue" (1024cores.net) — the ticket-based bounded ring with per-slot sequence numbers that achieves wait-free push/pop under single-producer/single-consumer restrictions; basis for boost::lockfree::bounded_ticket_queue and spsc_queue.

Paul E. McKenney, "Is Parallel Programming Hard?" — the definitive RCU reference covering memory ordering, grace-period algorithms, and safe reclamation for lock-free data structures; https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/RCU/.

Tim Blechmann et al., Boost.Lockfree — https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/master/doc/html/lockfree.html — implements queue (Michael-Scott MPMC), bounded_ticket_queue (Vyukov MPMC), mpsc_weak_queue, spsc_queue (ringbuffer), and spsc_value (triple buffer); covers wait-free vs lock-free configuration via single_producer/single_consumer policy tags.
Jeff Preshing, "Memory Reordering Explained" (preshing.com) — accessible treatment of acquire/release semantics, memory fences, and why relaxed ordering is a data race in disguise for lock-free code.

Martin Thompson et al., LMAX Disruptor — the high-performance inter-thread messaging pattern that replaced queues with a single-producer/multi-consumer ring buffer; described in "Disruptor: High Performance Inter-Thread Messaging" (2011) and https://lmax-exchange.github.io/disruptor/.
Herb Sutter, "Effective Concurrency" columns (Dr. Dobb's Journal) — practical guidance on lock-free design, the danger of composeability, and when to prefer serialized queues over lock-free ones.

Anthony Williams, C++ Concurrency in Action (2nd ed., 2019) — practical implementation of std::memory_order fences, std::atomic_thread_fence, and the C++20 atomics library used in production lock-free queues.

Hans Boehm, "Threads Cannot Be Implemented as a Library" (PLDI 2005) — clarifies why compiler optimizations can defeat hand-rolled lock-free code unless compiler barriers or proper memory orders are used.
Maged M. Michael and Michael L. Scott's canonical non-blocking queue pseudocode and origin history — https://www.cs.rochester.edu/research/synchronization/pseudocode/queues.html.

Oracle Java SE ConcurrentLinkedQueue documentation — describes the unbounded linked-node, non-blocking FIFO used by many concurrent producers and consumers: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/24/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ConcurrentLinkedQueue.html.

Microsoft Learn ConcurrentQueue<T> documentation — identifies the thread-safe FIFO as lock-free and documents its concurrent enqueue/dequeue API: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentqueue-1?view=net-9.0.

Rust crossbeam-queue documentation — documents bounded lock-free ArrayQueue and unbounded lock-free SegQueue, including their capacity tradeoff: https://docs.rs/crossbeam-queue/latest/crossbeam_queue/.

Are Your Epochs Too Epic? Batch Free Can Be Harmful — analyzes allocator contention and latency spikes caused by large epoch-reclamation batches in lock-free systems: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.11347.
